items.headline: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
items.blurb: Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez wants to defy the polls, and his main rivals accuse him of not telling the truth and of "betrayal".
items.text: Spain's main party leaders have held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez saying he is confident of defying the polls. "I cannot imagine us losing," he said, posing for selfies with supporters in red T-shirts and accusing conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo of planning a coalition with the far right. Feijóo's People's Party (PP) is narrowly ahead in the polls, and in the final hours of the campaign he travelled first to Barcelona and then Seville, promising voters a new political era of "truth, decency and good governance". He accused Sánchez of evading questions on key issues like corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt. The Socialist leader heads one of Europe's few left-wing governments, and with the French presidential elections five months away, there is a real chance that two of the continent's biggest economies could move to the right in quick succession. items.headline: Thousands of Puerto Ricans join ‘Day of National Outrage’ protest
items.blurb: Anger and frustration erupt over record-high electricity rates, surging cost of living and deteriorating basic services.
items.text: Thousands of Puerto Ricans have protested in the capital, San Juan, as anger and frustration erupted over record-high electricity rates, the surging cost of living, deteriorating basic services and other issues. Retirees, university students, bus drivers and others joined Friday’s protest organised by some 30 groups ranging from unions to religious organisations. The crowds gathered in front of a mall for what organisers dubbed the “Day of National Outrage”. Hundreds of demonstrators arrived by bus in San Juan from dozens of cities and towns across the island. Asked what problems Puerto Rico had, 74-year-old Radames Garcia Badillo said: “Where to start? The outrage is absolute.” He said that power and water services are unreliable and that his neighbourhood goes dark at least once a week for several hours. He also decried a sharp increase in the cost of living. “We’re buying less because things are extremely expensive,” he said. “For us retirees, it is essential to make every dollar stretch.” The protest, one of the largest in the US territory since Governor Jenniffer Gonzalez took office in January 2025, grew

items.text: What started as one artist’s response to being cut out of a music video has exploded, becoming a driving force in Nigeria’s cultural landscape A s a student in the central Nigerian city of Ilorin, Lawal Habeeb Kola loved staying in his hostel room to produce beats rather than returning to his family house in Lagos, the more frenetic city of his birth. In 2022, one of his beats became popular on TikTok, and a version featuring ad-libbed vocals from a hypeman sent it viral. He was invited to the music video shoot in Lagos and thought his big break had finally come, but when the video was released, he was absent. “I was in a restaurant and everybody was anticipating seeing me, but my face did not show once,” the 27-year old, known as DJ Khalipha, said. “I felt disgraced. I stopped posting the song.” Khalipha retreated to his dorm and revisited the DIY “cruise beats” genre of dance music that he had previously worked in. items.headline: Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
items.blurb: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks to end the war.
items.text: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying that delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough during peace talks. In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president also said it was "strange" that Donald Trump had posted a picture of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend". "Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English. "He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, suggesting it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during WWII. Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States. Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv. items.headline: Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter
items.blurb: Ukraine settles in for another devastating winter as the questions persists: how will it all end?
items.text: Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over. Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are. The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. items.headline: At least eight found dead on migrant boat off Spain’s Canary Islands
items.blurb: Six people airlifted to hospital in serious condition, Spanish rescue service says.
items.text: At least eight migrants have been found dead on a boat carrying about 100 people that was rescued near Spain’s Canary Islands, the Spanish maritime rescue service has said. The rescue service said on Friday that between eight and 10 bodies were found on board and that six people were airlifted to hospital in serious condition. The boat was found 39 nautical miles (72km) south of the island of El Hierro and was being towed to the port of La Estaca. Separately, 84 survivors from another boat came ashore at La Restinga, El Hierro’s main port, which has a reception centre and field hospital for migrants. The Canary Islands are a Spanish region in the Atlantic Ocean, off the coast of northwest Africa. Anyone who lands there reaches Spanish and European Union territory, which has made the islands a main entry point for migrants from West Africa. Arrivals hit a record of more than 46,000 in 2024 before falling after tighter surveillance and cooperation with countries of origin and transit. The blaze on the ring road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 25 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, the public prosecutor’s office said in a statement. At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video showed firefighters working to put out the fire spreading among the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene in the Warraq district of Imbaba, a Cairo suburb. The Egyptian president, Abdel-Fattah al-Sissi , expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement. items.text: Since New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos. "It was jarring," said Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make new arrangements for over 500 people. Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (£267,000) in just a few hours. Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday. On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds. The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action. items.headline: Law & politics: How 131st and 132nd Constitution amendment bills differ
items.blurb: The two bills replace the legislative framework that failed to secure the required two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha on April 17.
items.text: The Union government on Friday recast its constitutional amendment to guarantee a uniform 50% increase in Lok Sabha seats for every state and Union territory (UT), seeking to address the concerns of southern states that a population-based redistribution could diminish their political influence and demonstrating a significant rethink of its delimitation strategy after suffering an unprecedented defeat in Parliament in April. The Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill, 2026 and the Delimitation (Second) Bill, 2026, replace the legislative framework that failed to secure the required two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha on April 17. The provisions seek to retain the government’s central objective of implementing 33% reservation for women in Parliament and state assemblies before the 2029 general elections, but with an important political assurance now written into the Constitution — every state and Union territory will get 50% more seats than its existing allocation. The change addresses one of the principal criticisms of the earlier exercise, when Opposition parties argued that the government’s assurances of a uniform increase in representation were not reflected in the actual legislative provisions. items.headline: Bitcoin slips back below $60,000, missing out on Wall Street rally from Thanksgiving break
items.blurb: The divergence was particularly notable given that Bitcoin had advanced alongside US equity futures earlier in the day
items.text: Bitcoin fell back below $60,000 on Friday, missing out on a powerful rally in US equities as Wall Street returned from the Thanksgiving break. The largest cryptocurrency had earlier climbed as much as 2.3% to top $62,000 before reversing course, falling to a 24-hour low of around $58,760 as stock markets opened in New York . It subsequently traded around $59,900, even as the S&P 500 rallied 1.6%. Other cryptocurrencies also fell. The divergence was particularly notable given that Bitcoin had advanced alongside US equity futures earlier in the day, only to come under renewed selling pressure once stock markets opened. Cryptocurrencies have struggled to perform in recent weeks, with Bitcoin on track for its worst monthly performance in more than four years. The token is down roughly 23% in November, weakened by failing investor confidence after a series of major crypto hacks and mounting regulatory uncertainty following the US midterms. “A drop to $57,000 would signal a return to the short-term bearish scenario,” said Alex Kuptsikevich, chief market analyst at FxPro. items.headline: Faisal Islam: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
items.blurb: Other countries have rerouted trade in response to his first tariff salvo, now they are looking beyond Trump's tenure.
items.text: There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week. Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations. "We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC. Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda. The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April. items.headline: India Inc tightens third-party vendor checks over data breach liability ahead of DPDP Act deadline
items.blurb: From unapproved AI tools to sub-processor disclosures, companies are overhauling third-party risk checks before the May 2027 deadline.
items.text: NEW DELHI: Companies are tightening checks on vendors as they share more customer data with third-party service providers amid concerns over misuse and liability for breaches. They are asking why vendors need specific data and demanding clarity on storage, access and deletion ahead of India's 13 May 2027 compliance deadline under the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act. Organizations now want evidence rather than attestations: where data lives, how long it is kept, who else touches it and how fast a breach is reported, said Rajat Deshpande, co-founder and chief executive of third-party service provider FinBox. “Audit rights, deletion timelines and sub-processor disclosure are becoming standard terms rather than negotiated extras,” he said. Major enterprises in banking, fintech and consumer services act as data fiduciaries—entities that collect personal data—while outsourcing functions such as onboarding, verification, loan collections and customer support. Third-party service providers typically process that data on their behalf across multiple touchpoints outside the company's immediate control. items.headline: Foxtale’s income nearly doubles to Rs 400 Cr in FY26; losses narrow 10%
items.blurb: India’s skincare and beauty market has become increasingly competitive, with homegrown brands such as Minimalist, Innovist, Sugar Cosmetics and Foxtale vying for a larger share of the market.
items.text: India’s skincare and beauty market has become increasingly competitive, with homegrown brands such as Minimalist, Innovist, Sugar Cosmetics and Foxtale vying for a larger share of the market. While some brands have managed to scale their revenue and turn profitable, others continue to face pressure on their bottom lines. Amid this competition, Mumbai-based Foxtale reported a 93% year-on-year growth in operating revenue in the financial year ended March 2026, while its losses narrowed marginally by 10% to Rs 66 crore. According to its consolidated financial statements sourced from the Registrar of Companies (RoC), Foxtale's revenue from operations almost doubled to Rs 382.6 crore in FY26, compared with Rs 198.7 crore in FY25. Founded in 2021 by Romita Mazumdar, Foxtale is a direct-to-consumer skincare and beauty brand that focuses on products designed for Indian skin. Its portfolio includes products targeting concerns such as acne, ageing and hyperpigmentation. Sale of products remained the sole source of operating revenue for the company. It also earned Rs 17.6 crore in interest from bank deposits and investments, taking its total income to Rs 400 crore

items.headline: Decline of deities - the long game the All Blacks cannot afford to lose
items.blurb: Statistically, this generation of All Blacks is the weakest in decades. How has a sporting shorthand for success slipped so far?
items.text: Despite a population, player pool and bank balance smaller than most of their rivals, New Zealand's rugby team have become sporting shorthand for success. England beat the All Blacks this year and last. They play them again on Saturday aiming for a hat-trick. But, England would need that winning streak to continue until around 2050 just to level up a lop-sided historical head-to-head. New Zealand have won 36 times to England's 10 in their 121-year rivalry. For every other nation in Test rugby, the story is the same. New Zealand have the superior record against them all. A section on the All Blacks' website, titled Rivalries, , external opens by listing South Africa's 40% winning record in their meetings. And the numbers only drop from there. But New Zealand's grip on the global game appears looser now than ever. If they lose to England on Saturday, it may not much sway the historical balance between the two teams. items.text: You can have a good time brewing up widgets — as long as you don’t expect too much.﻿ You can have a good time brewing up widgets — as long as you don’t expect too much.﻿ Aside from dealing with my calendar , there’s one thing I want AI to do: tell me if I’m about to miss the bus. What I need is a widget. It needs to tell me real-time arrivals for the bus stop near my house. Tapping around on my phone screen to open the right app and select my stop will slow me down enough to miss a bus. I need glanceable information, and I hoped that Android’s vibe-coded widget feature could help me out here. It hasn’t, to my disappointment, but I still had a good time cooking up other widgets. items.headline: AI is straining America’s open records systems
items.blurb: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer.
items.text: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy. Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.” Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest.

items.headline: Grand Theft Auto VI proves why efficiency isn’t a virtue
items.blurb: On the same day that Anthropic entered the public market, a painstakingly human video game became one of most successful entertainment launches of all time.
items.text: It should have been impossible for “Grand Theft Auto VI” (GTA VI) to live up to the hype. Fans waited 13 years for the newest installment in the crime-adventure franchise, and Rockstar Games exceeded even those inconceivable expectations when the game finally came out last week. GTA VI launched as the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic and made $3.79 billion on release day to mark what could be the biggest entertainment event ever – more massive than “Avengers: Endgame” ( $2.9 billion ) or Taylor Swift’s Eras tour ( $2 billion ). The 13-year wait certainly fueled the frenzy, and sales, around GTA VI, but some fans craved GTA VI because of what it represents in the emerging era of AI. Even the biggest workaholics among us – startup founders – scheduled time off to play the game, including Spiry co-founder Dima Beseda , who told TechCrunch, “I reshuffled my workload to free up time around the weekends and even booked vitamin IV drips to keep my energy up.” Yet some players felt a sense of anticipatory nostalgia

items.headline: AI may soon change what it means to be a theoretical physicist
items.blurb: Frontier AI is already solving problems that once took top physicists a full day.
items.text: About six months ago, Suvrat Raju, a professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, India, asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem. He didn’t ask because he needed to know the answer. He had actually solved this particular problem already. But he had never published the solution—which made it a perfect question to test how good AI was at physics. LLMs have been trained on the whole Internet, so if a physics problem has been discussed online, it’s likely the model already knows about it and may have memorized the answer. So a fair test of AI capabilities needs to focus on problems that have never appeared online. The model didn’t answer Raju’s problem correctly, but it did better than he expected—well, enough to get him thinking that the experiment should be repeated and formalized. With the help of a colleague, he set out to create a theoretical physics benchmark for AI. items.blurb: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here. Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing.
items.text: Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well. Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm. This thinking isn’t all that fringe. items.blurb: Last year, Google filed a patent for a system called My Channel that's designed to create feeds filled with personalized, AI-generated videos and advertisements based on information the company knows about its users.
items.text: Imagine an endless feed of AI slop in which you are the main character of every story.﻿ Imagine an endless feed of AI slop in which you are the main character of every story.﻿ First spotted by Patentlyze , the patent — which was filed last May and published last week — describes how My Channel would use a person’s demographic data and viewing history to create its own prompts that would then be fed into an LLM to help generate AI videos tailored to that person’s specific interests. In addition to factoring in what kinds of videos a user tends to watch, the system would capture contextual data from their device like IP addresses, GPS locations, and specific details about the user’s age. My Channel could also base its prompts on current news like sports scores and things happening on social media, and all of the video generation would take place on Google’s servers. items.headline: What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?
items.blurb: A new AI-assisted proof seems to be solid, but we're not sure what it tells us.
items.text: Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis . The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset. It’s too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math. The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There’s not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. items.headline: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and ‘key man’ risks
items.blurb: The credit rating agency may lower Nvidia's credit rating to AA-, the fourth-highest rating.
items.text: S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices. Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P said in a statement . The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale. Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral. In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. In an announcement on Wednesday , the FCC says it authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million AI chip-equipped satellites as part of the Elon Musk-owned company’s “Starmind” initiative . With several others also pursuing the idea of putting AI data centers in space , including Google and Blue Origin, this is the first approval the agency has granted for a full “constellation” of AI satellites. The FCC’s approval requires SpaceX to deploy at least one satellite by 2033, and meet the 1 million satellite milestone by 2040. The FCC also deferred SpaceX’s request to dispose of satellites located above 600km in space “graveyard” orbits , rather than having them burn up in the Earth’s atmosphere, saying the company hasn’t provided “sufficient information” about its disposal process plans. items.headline: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
items.blurb: Most codes of conduct serve as a reflection of corporate culture. In Nvidia's case, that could have consequences.
items.text: When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired . “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO. It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. items.headline: Nvidia hits pause on chip shipments to Southeast Asia
items.blurb: Nvidia has told manufacturing partners to pause server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia as the U.S. tightens its push to keep AI chips out of China.
items.text: Nvidia is under pressure to do things differently, and a new WSJ report shows how far that’s going. According to the Journal, Nvidia has told manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to hit pause on server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia for an unspecified period as it assesses whether its regional partners are meeting U.S. export requirements. As for why those countries, Chinese companies have been tapping Nvidia chips remotely from data centers there, a loophole the US Commerce Department closed — reportedly grudgingly — earlier this month. The Journal notes that the think tank Institute for Progress estimates remote data centers like these supply about 24% of China’s AI computing power.

items.headline: Tidal announces ban on AI-generated music; 27 million tracks will be deleted
items.blurb: AI songs account for 6.3 percent of Tidal's catalog, but it's about to be zero.
items.text: Most streaming music providers have opted to label AI-generated content on their platforms, and until now, Tidal was one of them. However, the company is about to take a harder stance. Tidal announced that in the coming weeks, it will fully ban AI music because of the harm it does to human artists. Tidal debuted its initial AI policy in July 2026, which included labeling and demonetizing all songs created entirely with AI. That wasn’t enough to stem the tide of AI slop, though. Over the past 90 days, Tidal reports that 43 percent of new uploads were completely AI-generated. On November 6, new uploads to Tidal hit a whopping 60 percent AI-generated. As things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million tracks labeled as AI, all of which were obviously added in the past couple of years. That accounts for 6.3 percent of Tidal’s total catalog. On December 9, Tidal will delete all those songs. The streamer notes this will have essentially no negative impact, because 96 percent of AI-labeled tracks got zero plays in the past 90 days. items.headline: How Trump and Silicon Valley forced Nvidia to take Jensen Huang back
items.blurb: Huang’s allies enlisted Trump and Vance to pressure Nvidia’s board into taking him back.
items.text: On Monday morning, Jensen Huang walked into Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters to rapturous applause from employees lining the walkways above him. Huang was visibly moved as one colleague threw themselves into his arms for a hug. The spectacular reinstatement of the chief executive of Nvidia, less than two weeks after he resigned in a scandal over an affair with a customer and suspected Chinese spy—as well as a second reported affair with a subordinate—caught even the company’s most senior executives by surprise. The abrupt reversal by Nvidia’s board was spurred by President Donald Trump, who applied pressure to the board over the weekend after watching what was once America’s most valuable company as well as the wider tech sector haemorrhage value last week. It was the culmination of frenetic lobbying by a “war room” of Huang’s Silicon Valley allies, who pulled in Trump and vice-president JD Vance, according to people familiar with the events. items.headline: Want to buy your kid an AI toy this Christmas? Not in New York
items.blurb: New York has banned AI chatbot toys for five years as new research from Common Sense Media reveals troubling safety failures, including exposure to inappropriate content and risks to emotional development.
items.text: Santa won’t be delivering any AI chatbot toys to New York kids this Christmas. Gov. Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years. The bill explicitly targets toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, like talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that rely on the internet to keep kids yapping. The bill makes New York the second state after California to institute a ban on AI toys. Technically, the new law takes effect 90 days after signing, so some parents could try to fulfill their kids’ wish lists for a creepy toy like a jumped-up Furby in time for the holidays, but the governor urges them not to, given the risks. items.text: Founded by Freshworks alumni, Dreamteam is building an AI-native CRM platform that uses four AI agents and a central context layer called Company Brain to automate sales workflows. The startup has over 100 customers across 13 countries and aims to become an eight-figure revenue business by the end of 2027. Dreamteam raised $53 Mn from Together Fund, Accel and Premji Invest in November to strengthen its product, engineering and go-to-market operations, as it takes on established CRM players such as Salesforce, HubSpot and Zoho. In B2B sales, customer relationship management (CRM) is as old as fire. It encompasses the strategies and software tools businesses use to track, manage and improve customer interactions. While the technology has evolved over the years, AI is bringing about a more fundamental shift in how businesses use it. AI tools in CRM can automate routine tasks, personalise customer interactions, and streamline sales workflows. items.text: Dunzo cofounder Kabeer Biswas’ AI startup M has raised $9 Mn (₹82 Cr) in a fresh funding round led by VC firm RTP Global, sources familiar with the development told Inc42. Existing investors of the startup, including Peak XV Partners and Blume Ventures, also doubled down on their erstwhile bets. With this fundraise, M’s total capital raised has reached around $20 Mn. Queries sent to M, RTP Global, and Blume Ventures didn’t receive any response till the time of publication. The story would be updated based on receiving their responses. The latest round comes around seven months after M raised $11 Mn (around ₹102 Cr) in a seed funding round led by Peak XV, with participation from Blume Ventures and fintech major CRED. Founded in December 2025 by Biswas and former Swish executive Kartik Mishra, M currently offers access through a waitlist.
